title: Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee March 17-18, 2026
summary: The FOMC minutes from March 17-18, 2026 reveal a Committee grappling with conflicting pressures: Middle East conflict-driven energy shocks pushing inflation expectations higher, while AI-related disruptions weighed on growth outlooks. Market pricing shifted markedly higher for the near-term rate path, with options now implying approximately 30% probability of rate hikes through early next year. PCE inflation remained elevated at 2.8% in January, and oil front-month futures surged approximately 50% over the intermeeting period.
key_points: PCE inflation stood at 2.8% in January 2026, remaining elevated; total CPI data appears truncated in source
Front-month crude oil futures increased approximately 50% over the intermeeting period due to Middle East conflict
Market-implied federal funds rate path shifted higher, with rate cut not fully priced in until December 2026
Options prices imply approximately 30% probability of rate hikes through early 2027; distribution of outcomes became more dispersed
Desk Survey respondents still expected two 25bp cuts this year, though market intelligence suggests some shifted toward fewer cuts after survey
Broad equity prices fell approximately 5% over the period; software sector underperformed notably due to AI-related concerns
Standing repo operations reached $30 billion on one day (third-largest volume since inception), suggesting increased willingness to use operations
Reserves projected to average approximately $3 trillion through September 2026 after April tax payment trough
why_it_matters: These minutes capture the Fed's assessment amid a significant energy price shock from the Middle East conflict, which forced a recalibration of the inflation outlook. The divergence between market pricing (no cuts until December, 30% hike probability) and the Desk Survey (two cuts still expected) highlights policy uncertainty. The 50% oil spike and persistent 2.8% PCE inflation constrain Fed easing room while AI disruptions create growth headwinds—a stagflationary mix.
macro_context: The Middle East conflict emerged as the primary macro catalyst during the intermeeting period, driving a 50% spike in oil prices and elevating near-term inflation expectations. The one-year inflation swap rate rose nearly 50 basis points, while longer-horizon inflation compensation remained little changed—suggesting markets view the shock as potentially transitory. AI disruptions weighed on technology and software sectors, with leveraged loan prices for software firms declining sharply. Global central banks (ECB, BoC, SNB) previously expected to remain on hold or ease are now expected to hike rates modestly. Dollar sentiment turned more positive on safe-haven demand and energy exporter status.
market_structure_context: Treasury market liquidity diminished modestly in line with increased yield volatility but continued to function well. Money market conditions remained broadly stable; the effective federal funds rate held 1 basis point below IORB, and repo rates stayed near IORB. Overnight reverse repo usage was minimal except at month-ends. Standing repo operations were used on only a couple of settlement-heavy days, with the $30 billion usage on one day (third-largest ever) suggesting increased comfort with these facilities following December 2024 changes. The manager assessed reserves as remaining within the ample range.
